summary:
FieldShift: NASA Data for Climate-Smart Crop Rotations

FieldShift is a web app that helps farmers choose crop rotations that save water, rebuild soil, and cut pollution. A farmer picks a field anywhere on Earth. The app then combines NASA Earth observations (POWER, SMAP, GRACE-FO, IMERG, MODIS/VIIRS, FIRMS, MERRA-2, NEX-GDDP-CMIP6) with ISRIC SoilGrids data, crop traits, and the farmer’s own priorities, such as profit, water saving, and soil health.

It ranks rotations from 0 to 100 and explains each score. A what-if simulator tests them against weaker monsoons, extreme heat, and groundwater decline. A stubble calculator compares open burning with alternatives like Happy Seeder and baling. The app also generates a printable action plan in English, Hindi, and Punjabi, with voice and offline modes for smallholders.

It matters because groundwater depletion, extreme heat, and crop-residue smoke threaten food security and health worldwide. In our Sangrur, Punjab case study, a 100-farm village at 60% adoption saves about 702 million litres of groundwater a year and prevents 4.3 tonnes of PM2.5 smoke. FieldShift turns free, open NASA data into decisions a farmer can act on this week.
details:
FieldShift: Project Details

What it does and how it works

FieldShift is a decision-support web app that helps farmers explore crop rotations that conserve water, strengthen soil, and reduce pollution. It works in seven steps:

  1. Field setup. The farmer picks a location by map or coordinates, then enters the standing crop, past rotations, irrigation type, and tubewell depth. Soil properties (pH, organic carbon, sand and clay, nitrogen, salinity) load automatically from ISRIC SoilGrids and can be overridden with a Soil Health Card.
  2. Priorities. Sliders (0-5) cover profit, water saving, soil health, low pollution, low risk, and low labour cost. Constraints include “must include wheat for the household” and the machinery available through Custom Hiring Centres.
  3. NASA field dashboard. It shows temperature and heat-stress days (POWER), soil moisture (SMAP), groundwater trend (GRACE-FO), rainfall (IMERG), crop vigour and fallow gaps (MODIS/VIIRS), evapotranspiration versus rainfall, and 2030/2050 climate scenarios (NEX-GDDP-CMIP6).
  4. Pollution and stubble monitor. FIRMS fire detections and MERRA-2 PM2.5 and AOD feed a calculator. It compares open burning with Happy Seeder, baling, and in-situ mulching, in kg of PM2.5, kg of CO₂e, and fine risk.
  5. Rotation recommender. A multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) model scores each rotation from 0 to 100 using the farmer’s weights. Every score comes with positive drivers, agronomic risks, a season calendar, and this week’s actions.
  6. What-if simulator. Sliders for monsoon deficit, temperature rise, groundwater drop, and a stubble-ban toggle re-rank the rotations live, so farmers can see which choice holds up under stress.
  7. Action plan and community impact. A printable one-page advisory card, a WhatsApp-style briefing, and a 100-farm village calculator.

Benefits

  • Farmers get ranked options with clear reasons, not a black-box answer.
  • It shows the trade-offs between income, water, soil carbon, and smoke side by side.
  • It gives a practical alternative to burning straw.
  • It works for low-literacy and low-connectivity users, with Hindi, Punjabi, and English, voice read-out, high-contrast mode, large touch targets, and offline data.

Intended impact

In our Sangrur, Punjab case study, 60% of a 100-farm village moving from rice-wheat to maize-wheat-summer moong saves about 702 million litres of groundwater a year. It also prevents 4.3 tonnes of PM2.5 smoke and saves 64.8 MWh of pumping power and ₹16.65 lakh in farm costs (these are the figures the app shows at 60% adoption). The architecture takes only latitude and longitude, so the same approach extends to other regions facing water stress and residue burning.

Tools and technology

  • Frontend: React 18, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, react-i18next, and the Web Speech API for voice.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI, with separate engines for scoring, water balance, and pollution.
  • Methods: FAO-56 crop water balance, IPCC emission factors, and MCDA scoring.
  • Data: NASA POWER, SMAP, GRACE/GRACE-FO, GPM IMERG, MODIS/VIIRS, MODIS/ECOSTRESS ET, FIRMS, MERRA-2, NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, plus ISRIC SoilGrids and our own crop library.
  • Quality and deployment: automated pytest tests (12 passing), Docker and docker-compose, and bundled offline datasets.
  • AI assistance: we used an AI coding agent (Google Antigravity) to help generate and iterate on the code, and the team directed the design and reviewed the results.

What makes it creative

  • It links NASA’s water, fire, air, and climate datasets to one farmer decision: what to grow next.
  • Every recommendation is transparent and tied to the data behind it.
  • The stubble calculator treats burning as one option to compare, not a problem to lecture about.
  • The 100-farm village view turns individual choices into collective impact.

Factors we considered

  • Data honesty: each panel shows its source and resolution. GRACE-FO is a coarse (~300 km) regional signal, not a well-level reading, and MERRA-2 PM2.5 is modelled, not measured.
  • Resilience: rotations are tested against future climate and worst-case shocks, not only average conditions.
  • Local rules and feasibility: sowing windows, regulations such as Punjab’s subsoil water and stubble-burning rules, machinery access, and food-security needs.
  • Accessibility: language, literacy, and connectivity.
  • Limits: this is an advisory tool, and farmers should confirm major changes with their local agricultural extension service (KVK/PAU in Punjab).
